Title: A Landmark in Fantasy Filmmaking
Description:
Few films achieve what The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring manages to do-transporting audiences to an entirely new world with such depth and authenticity. Peter Jackson's adaptation of J. R. R. Tolkien's legendary novel is an incredible achievement, building a rich mythology, introducing a massive ensemble cast, and immersing us in the breathtaking landscapes of Middle-earth.

What makes this film particularly remarkable is that, even nearly 25 years after its release, its world-building remains unparalleled. The scale of the sequences, the intricacy of the special effects, and the tangible sense of adventure make it feel groundbreaking even today. Before this film, few movies had created such a vast and immersive fantasy world where every detail-both visual and narrative-feels fully realized.

One of the film's greatest strengths is how it balances fantasy with realism. The opening 30 minutes are dedicated to the mundane life of the hobbits, establishing the simplicity of their world and how far removed they are from adventure. This slow, deliberate introduction makes the stakes feel higher once they are thrust into the larger conflict. At the same time, the film seamlessly weaves in the history of Middle-earth, laying the groundwork for the dangers to come. The contrast between the peaceful Shire and the perilous journey ahead makes the adventure feel grander and the characters' transformations more impactful.

Beyond character development, the film's world-building is enhanced by its stunning cinematography. While CGI plays a role, much of the film was shot on location in New Zealand, giving Middle-earth an organic, lived-in feel. Sweeping shots of mountains, vast fields, and grand fortresses make this world feel vast and real. The film's use of practical effects-such as forced perspective to make Elijah Wood appear smaller-further enhances the illusion, blending technical innovation with classic filmmaking techniques.

Another key factor in the film's success is its stellar casting. While many of the actors were not major stars at the time, they embody their roles so perfectly that it's now impossible to imagine anyone else playing them. The performances breathe life into the characters, making them feel fully realized beyond just their archetypal roles in a fantasy epic.

The emotional depth of the characters is also a highlight. The film doesn't just tell a story about wizards and hobbits-it explores universal themes of temptation, redemption, and sacrifice. Boromir's arc, for example, is particularly powerful. His internal struggle with the lure of the Ring is compelling because his motivations are understandable. He wants to protect his people, but in doing so, he nearly succumbs to the same corruption that has destroyed so many others. This nuanced portrayal of temptation makes the story resonate on a deeply human level.

If there's one drawback to The Fellowship of the Ring, it's the necessity of condensing such a large and detailed novel into a three-hour runtime. This film, more than the others in the trilogy, has to juggle the enormous task of establishing the world, introducing key characters, and moving the plot forward. At times, this leads to a rushed feeling as the story compresses major events into a tight narrative. However, considering the complexity of the source material, the adaptation is still remarkably effective.

When taken as a whole, The Fellowship of the Ring is nothing short of a cinematic triumph. It sets the stage for one of the most ambitious trilogies ever made, blending cutting-edge technology with classic storytelling to create an unforgettable experience. More than just an adaptation, it captures the essence of Tolkien's world while making it feel real, lived-in, and emotionally resonant. It's a film that continues to inspire and captivate, proving that truly great fantasy storytelling stands the test of time.

Title: My Thoughts on One of My Favourite Films
Description:
There are so many reviews and critical analysis already written about Peter Jackson's adaptation of Tolkien's epic literary masterpiece that adding my own feels almost redundant.

However, I want to contribute my own few words of appreciation. Because how couldn't I? Jackson's trilogy has left such a marked impression on my life, such a lasting influence, that I am still obsessed to this day after the first time I have watched it at the cinema with my family more than two decades ago. The Tolkien purist might argue there are certain mistakes. But there is no arguing against the sheer quality, the sheer magnitude of the jaw-droppingly awesome cinematic and epic mastery of this trilogy, of which 'The Fellowship of the Ring', while it lacks the war scenes of the following titles, is no exception to.

I adore Jackson's adaptations of 'The Lord of the Rings' franchise and I honestly rate 'The Fellowship of the Ring' as one of my favourites and one of the most influential films of my life.

Title: Middle Earth Adventures
Description:
In the early 1930s, John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon studies at Oxford University. In his spare time, he amused himself by writing fantastic stories for his four young children. One of these tales, "The Hobbit", was read by an English publisher who suggested Tolkien make the story available in book form. To everyone's surprise, the novel became a huge success (the first edition sold out in less than a month). So, the publisher asked Tolkien to write a sequel, which the professor grudgingly agreed to. But it wasn't easy. Almost twenty years would pass before Tolkien was able to complete his work. By now, the book was called "The Lord of the Rings".

Bringing Tolkien's masterpiece to the screen proved to be more difficult than anyone could have imagined. After several years of negotiations, United Artists managed to buy the rights to "The Lord of the Rings" in 1976. Animator Ralph Bakshi then produced a film that covered the first half of the trilogy. But that's where it stopped. The work was suspended indefinitely after scores of disappointed fans complained that Bakshi's version didn't really match Tolkien's original story.

Fortunately, things improved when Peter Jackson took over. The New Zealander had just formed his own special effects company and together with his technicians he was able to conjure up all the orcs, hobbits and goblins Tolkien's story is filled with. And, of course, the breathtaking landscape of New Zealand helped. It transported the audience to a remote fantasy world where anything could happen.

Still, everyone's nerves were on edge before the film's premiere. After all, the Internet was abuzz with people who complained about all the changes Peter Jackson had made to their beloved trilogy. Fortunately, there was no need to worry. As "The Lord of the Rings" opened in London, New York and Los Angeles, it was evident that the picture was a huge success. Consequently, even the die-hard Tolkien fans turned out in droves.

Title: An amazing First Step Into This Rich Fantasy World, Expertly Crafted by Peter Jackson
Description: An amazing miracle of an adaptation that beautifully brings JR Tolkien's classic story to life on the big screen. Everyone is cast perfectly and they all bring so much personality and uniqueness to their roles; Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins, Ian McKellan as Gandalf, Christopher Lee as Saruman, Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn, Orlando Bloom as Legolas, John Rhys-Davis as Gimli, Ian Holm as Bilbo Baggins, Cate Blanchett as Gadriel, Andy Serkis's brief cameo as Gollum, and Sean Astin as Samwise (aka the underrated MVP of the franchise). The sets are gorgeously crafted, combined with the scenic wilds of New Zealand that truly bring this epic fantasy setting to life. Howard Shore's music is iconically epic and sweeps with emotion with its numerous leitmotifs tailored for each character and setting (the Shire being my favorite). The special effects hold up phenomenally well, thanks to its responsible balance between practical and digital effects to bring us the best of both worlds. Convincing, yet grand and epic in scale. The movie definitely takes its time in the beginning to get the story going (there's also some weird audio mixing and awkward camera angles early on). But the fantasy worldbuilding and the Shire are so charming, you don't mind spending a little extra time getting settled into the everyday routine of this world before the adventure begins. The calm before the storm. Getting enriched with the peaceful setting to really hammer home what's at stake when Sauron threatens that peace. That epic opening scene greatly sets the tone and stakes. After the long prologue, you get a real sense of adventure as the stakes keep getting raised as Gandalf sends Frodo & his fellow Hobbits on a quest to destroy the ring. From walking the furthest they've ventured out of their small village, to getting attacked by nazguls, to making new allies at the shady bar, to gathering the iconic fellowship at the Elf safe haven. That's not even getting into their new quest to cross the mountains into the mines and out the river. All while Saruman is building a new army of orcs, with some subtle commentary on industrialization plundering the wilderness to feed the war machine as a nice homage to Britain in WWI. The ring itself is a great character, with so much mystery and tension thanks to the clever cinematography and carefully sized props. And you feel such a comradery between the Fellowship. It's a shame they're all split up for the next 2 movies, even if it's for the best for their individual character arcs. The ending climax is very exciting and ends on such an exciting cliffhanger that changes everything for the Trilogy. It's not the most epic of the Trilogy, but it's certainly the most personal. It truly is lightning in a little with the right people using the write effects and cast at the right time to perfectly translate this immensely grand world to life.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
Description:
Movie Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring Director: Peter Jackson Starring: Elijah Wood, Viggo Mortensen, Ian McKellen, Orlando Bloom, Sean Astin The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is a majestic and thrilling adventure that sets the stage for one of the most epic trilogies in cinematic history. Peter Jackson's masterful direction brings J. R. R. Tolkien's beloved novel to life with breathtaking landscapes, memorable characters, and heart-pumping action sequences.

The film follows Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood), a young hobbit tasked with destroying the One Ring and saving Middle-earth from the dark lord Sauron. Joined by a fellowship of brave and noble companions, including Gandalf the Grey (Ian McKellen), Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), Legolas (Orlando Bloom), Gimli (John Rhys-Davies), and Boromir (Sean Bean), Frodo embarks on a perilous journey across treacherous mountains, dark forests, and treacherous rivers.

The cast delivers outstanding performances, with standout turns from McKellen, Mortensen, and Wood. The chemistry between the actors is palpable, making the fellowship's camaraderie and conflicts all the more believable and engaging.

Jackson's direction is equally impressive, balancing action, drama, and humor with ease. The film's pacing is well-balanced, with a narrative that flows smoothly and never feels rushed or dragging.

The real star of the show, however, is Middle-earth itself. Jackson's use of New Zealand's stunning landscapes, combined with impressive set design and special effects, transports viewers to a richly detailed and immersive world.

Overall, The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is a masterpiece of epic storytelling, with a richly detailed world, memorable characters, and thrilling action sequences. It's a must-see for fans of fantasy and adventure, and a fitting start to one of the greatest trilogies in cinematic history.

Title: Fantastic movie a 10/10
Description:
An absolutely gorgeous adaptation of J. R. R. Tolkien's first LORD OF THE RINGS installment detailing how well-meaning young hobbit Wood unwittingly inherits a ring from his adventurous uncle Holm which possesses a dark force that is powerful enough to end all life in Middle-Earth. Visually wondrous even for those who aren't that into the fantasy genre. This installment is particularly charming for less action and more character development and, for some reason, the Middle-Earth lingo works really well in this movie over the second and third films. Although FELLOWSHIP merely teases the viewer with the appearance of Gollum-while TWO TOWERS and RETURN are basically owned by Serkis as Tolkien's timelessly wretched creature who's not quite friend or foe-the movie is just too lovable to really even need his inclusion. McKellen is perfect as Gandalf the Grey, and Bean's performance brings to the foreground the genius of all these characters who suffers from similar temptations and weaknesses that we do in reality. It is FELLOWSHIP that holds the clearest mirror up to us, while the following two films kind of just linger in the wartime aftermath. The greatest fantasy film of all-time.

Truly a masterpiece.

Title: Awesome,incredible movie
Description:
...but oh was I thankful for it!!! All through the movie I kept on having this big large smile sculpted into my face. For the record, I'm 25 years old, and I've read "The Lord of the Rings" in three times for the first time when I was six or seven years old. Ever since then, I read it at least once or twice a year - therefore you can count me as a fan, for I follow the same cult fan procedure with "The Hobbit" and "The Silmarillion" as well. Now onto the movie... Gosh, I saw it more than one time, and I keep wanting more of it. It just never gets boring! I really enjoyed the little stuff that is found throughout the movie for fans of the books (the map on Bilbo's table in his house comes to mind, it is exactly as the one in "The Hobbit" book that I own), and I also incredibly enjoyed the intro sequence with the re-telling of the battle against Sauron from the Silmarillion, never has an ultimate evil being been so well depicted on the screen. It truly is Sauron.

Those who argue the movie cuts too many parts or that it changes the story too much are totally wrong. This movie could not have shown the whole first time in its entirety - keep in mind that the audiobook version of 'Fellowship of the Ring' lasts well over ten hours, making a movie this long would, well, make it way too long and besides, how would you financially sustain such a project? I've read a reviewer saying he'd make all three books with the time allowed for the first movie alone. I think it would be a very fast-forwarding experience of a movie with 'Alvin and the Chimpmunks' kind of voices, incredibly stupid to say the least.

Ok, so there are changes in the movie - well, this is Jackson's vision of it. All of us have our own visions of the books, which may or may not be compatible with that of Jackson's, but I can safely assume that nobody can say they have a hundred percent the same vision of the story as Tolkien; that's the thing with books: each reader has a different vision of it. As for me, I was blown away. Never before have I felt so much at home in a movie, it is as if I had taken a walk in the town where I grew up, the Shire, Rivendell, Moria, Lorien, everything felt so much like home, I was moved. I cannot tell of another movie that had me shed tears just by seeing a landscape on screen.

Title: barely met expectations
Description: First of all, LOTR isn't a bad movie at all. In fact I find it pretty good. But can a movie meet such high expectations? I don't think so...too many people have been waiting too long for this movie. A LOTR mania is about to start. Here are some brief remarks of what I thought of the movie: First of all, the settings, landscapes, characters, camera work and overall art direction are great. Well taken care of, like you would expect from a movie with this big-a-budget. The story is kept in tact, and the thee hours pass in no-time. My only 'problem' is: if you make a mix between 13th warrior, the Neverending Story, Dragonheart, Braveheart, Gladiator and the Mummy you'll end up with the same result. It's a good movie because the makers had to guts to make a movie about such world renowned books...but the movie itself doesn't come up with anything new or shocking.

Title: Good Story, Bad Movie
Description:
Now don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the movie. The story is incredible in book and on screen, but the Screen Adaptation was lackluster. The jokes and the drama were pretty cheezy in a lot of places. They still worked, but for a classic like the LOtR Trilogy I would hope for a more mature movie.

And the cinematography was wretched. They repeated the same over-done, helicopter-circling-establishing-shot every time the fellowship came to a new location. The action scenes were largely shot in the hand-held, up close style and while I admit there is some use for this, it is hardly original, and I think we would prefer to actually SEE the action!

And the character's sizes were all wacked out...I understand it was hard to make big people into little people, but for the amount of money put into this movie I think the sizes could have been constant.

But as I said it was a great story, I loved watching the movie, I just wish it had been done by a more capable director+crew.

Title: Great eye candy, however story lacks peaks and valleys
Description:
Just got home from seeing this movie. Let me start off by saying the cinematography is fantastic, and the special effects are awesome. But that's pretty much where it stopped impressing me.

With all the hype about this film, the storyline has all but been fully revealed, thus not leaving many surprises. The plot never really took me up very high and failed to drop me to any depths. I felt that it lacked any highs and lows, and rather continued on a flat journey. (visually, a very impressive journey - but as far as the storyline went, I wasn't all that impressed) What I'm trying to say is that I really didn't become very attached to any of the characters, and therefore couldn't really have sympathy for them during their losses and didn't feel very rewarded during their triumphs.

I do feel that the high ratings it has received is largely due to the spectacular special effects, very impressive computer animation, and breathtaking scenery. (which is why I gave it a 7/10) While it's certainly no Star Wars (New Hope, Empire, and Jedi all get 10/10 in my book) or Braveheart (another 10); VISUALLY it is an excellent film.

I will be anxious to see what they give us in the next two...

Just my $.02 so please keep the flames to a min. =)

Description: The promotion of this movie is a fraud. I walked into this movie believing it was a fantasy but found I was in a never-ending, 3 hour nightmare. This movie is not for children or adults of weak constitution. I can't count the number of people slaughtered but it must be in the thousands. It is so bad I am reminded of `Conan the Barbarian' but at least with that movie I expected it. The endless decapitations and severed appendages are truly disturbing. Beyond the carnage are the truly horrible scenes of monsters right out of your worst nightmare. I am sure many people who see it will have nightmares for years to come. But the biggest disappointment of all is that it does not come to a conclusion  it just abruptly ends leaving you with the dilemma of suffering through the next two installments to see the conclusion. This is something I will never do. There is one saving grace and that is that it is well made and well acted. Unfortunately, this cannot overcome the nightmare.

Title: The movie is terrible.
Description: I'm a die-hard Lord of the Rings fan. I read the books for the first time over 30 years ago. I've read it over 50 times - including once out loud to my daughter when she was a little girl. I was very, very excited about seeing the movie. However, it turned out to be a major disappointment. Actually, it's much worse than that - I'm heartbroken. They cut an incredible amount of stuff, added a bunch of garbage that Tolkien never wrote and significantly changed many of the parts that they did see fit to leave in. At least I don't have to worry about seeing the next two - this one is so bad that there is no way I would ever go to see the next ones. I'd pay money to avoid seeing the next two and double to get out of the theater if I entered by mistake!

Title: Shockingly triumphant! The BEST film of 2001! No question!
Description: December 18 was a pretty normal day for me to begin with. I looked in the paper and saw in the film listings that a midnight showing of "The Fellowship of the Ring" would take place that evening. I quickly called people and asked if they would like to join me and they said, without hesitation, "yes". I bought six tickets in all, and the rest of my day was filled with anticipation. After arriving at approximately 11:15pm, I could tell this would be something special just from the quantity of people ready to set their eyes on a masterpiece. After 30 min. of trailers, the film began and there was an aura af astoundment and joy flowing through the dark room. Rare was a person that was fidgeting or going to the bathroom or concession stand or anything like that. The images on the screen startled the mind, and 3 quarters of the way through the film, you'd already gone through every emotion thinkable with it: anger, joy, love, sadness, excitement, amusement, everything. It is by this time, the first time you see the movie, you're overwhelmed by the eye candy, emotional intensity, adrenaline rushes during the action scenes, and best of all, the sweeping narrative and STELLAR acting. The cast could not have been so impeccable as this one. Let me just say that, if I had my way, EVERY cast member would earn an acting Oscar. Peter Jackson has made an engaging film that challenges, entertains, and best of all: tells a story. There is an equal balance of CGI and live effects in the film, so that seeing something spectacular doesn't seem boring. Shore's score is awesome, and the cinematography is positively astounding. In the theatre, when the credits rolled on the screen, everyone in the place was entranced by what they just saw, and everyone in the theatre was p****d they had a wait a year to see more. I could have not asked for a better movie! The best film of the year! SEE IT!! SEE IT AGAIN!! 10/10

Title: um
Description:
While Lord of the Rings is one of the most widely known and loved movie and book franchises in the world, it is not the movie for me. I can recognize why it's so popular, it brought a new standard for special effects to the 2000's and a classic book to life. However, after enduring four hours of little men with hairy feet panicking over a ring, I believe it's slightly overrated.

This isn't the most ground-breaking movie ever created but it does deserve a substantial amount of credit. I have watched both the extended and non- extended version and neither were very riveting, despite being adventure stories. As someone who is not the biggest fan of the fantasy genre, this movie was very hard to get into. The most entertaining part of the movie was Frodo's facial expressions and the 2001 fighting scene special effects. The extended version even threw in some questionable and off-putting extreme close ups of Gandalf's face and hobbit feet. However, there is something to be said for the number of movies the Lord of The Rings influenced after its release and the attention to detail within the franchise. It had some exceptionally stunning shots and the complex world building carried from the book to the movie was well executed. Although I don't wish to ever watch this movie again, I acknowledge that it unearthed a new side to fantasy that raised the bar significantly.

Title: It's not as good as people praise it to be
Description: After having this movie on my watchlist for years, I finally gave it a chance with an open mind. My expectations were high because people often claim it to be the greatest movie trilogy of all time. However, after investing almost an hour in the movie, I realized it simply wasn't my cup of tea. There was no meaningful symbolism, character development, or strong dialogue. The plot felt dull, and I didn't feel any emotional connection to the characters-no character death made me feel even a little sad. In the end, I'd say it's a good movie for kids, but it just wasn't for me and i still forced myself to watch it.

Title: The Standard For All Fantasy Films
Description: Lord of The Rings is, to me, the industry standard for fantasy films. That being said, it doesn't particularly resonate with me personally. Despite the strongly communicated themes of the virtues of bravery and fellowship, the downfall of this film (and book it's based off) is its worldbuilding. LOTR makes use of "hard world building", the narrator (or in this case the director) is very explicit in their worldbuilding, you directly see their vision through the inclusion of many details and direct explanations of events, characters, and places. LOTR uses this to great success, sadly it just doesn't resonate that well with me. I prefer the opposite, "soft worldbuilding", implicitly building the world leaving more up to interpretation. I don't mean to say that soft worldbuilding is objectively better, it's just my preference. This is why Lord of The Rings isn't really my type of movie, despite this I still think it's objectively good, the cinematics shine through here, the use of wide shots really encapsulates the scope of the world that this story takes place in, something I did really appreciate. The characters are also great, so all in all I do really think this movie set the bar for fantasy films in Hollywood. But again, it just doesn't really appeal to my preferences.

Title: Frodo ruins it
Description: I have seen The Hobbit six times and The Lord if the Rings twice only because Frodo is the most useless and annoying character in this entire saga. He is weak and not a good judge of character. Anytime some minor inconvenience arises he lies down and goes into a shock. Between gollum and Sam he chose gollum. And thanks to gollum the Ring was destroyed otherwise he was taking it back. What part of this entire journey was heroic for him?

Title: The tide has turned??
Description:
Where were all these negative reviews when i bought my ticket?? :) Honestly, it was a fine adaptation, on par or slightly above your average great-book-turned-good-movie-but-not-quite-enough film. Let's be honest-- we expected too much and got suckered juuuuuust a bit. That being said, i enjoyed the movie. Beginning was slow, Bilbo was by far the best actor in the movie, his scenes were the best. The Balrog scene and the proceeding scene were absolutely stunning. The rest was really good. My big gripe?

**** SPOILER ****

i invest 3 hours of my life into this movie, come to terms with its minor flaws, and what line do the three hunters leave me on?? i believe it was aragorn saying... wait for it... "LET'S HUNT SOME ORC!!" I mean JESUS!!! Did they hire the screenwriter from Rambo just for that line?? ruined the movie for me and left the bad taste in my mouth that prompted this negatively leaning review.

**** END SPOILER ****

I still liked the movie. Love John Rhys Davies, love Hugo Weaving, love Cate Blanchette, LOVE Sir Ian McKellen. All in all didn't mind the Arwen thing. I guess that's it... oh, Samwise. Fantastic. that was the one character i was NOT looking forward to. (Mikey from the Goonies?? in LOTR?!?? please...) Sean was really great. I guess that wraps it up.
